THE FOUNDING AND GROWTH OF SAVOY

THE FOUNDER OF SAVOY.—The town of Savoy, which was founded in 1872, derived its classic name from its founder, William Louis Marshall Savoy, better known as Colonel William Savoy. He was born in Mississippi in 1818, and received a liberal education including training in modern languages which he never applied in practice.⁹

Colonel Savoy came to Texas when he was a very young man and settled at Bonham. The town bearing his name is not yet known as the Savoy Plantation.

Colonel Savoy was a man of adventurous spirit. In 1849 he joined the crowd in the California gold rush, making his trip to water, a professional scout. He was stricken with pick and shovel and brought back to Texas golden nuggets in a heavy commercial way.

During the Civil War Colonel Savoy enlisted in the Confederate Army, at least at a captain, but he received a wound in his foot which kept him out of active service. For the next few years he travelled on the Missouri-Pacific and the Pacific three times. His daughter, Mrs. Ada Savoy Travis, thinks the travelling was in connection with the Pony Service. She recalls that her father related many of his experiences in her when he was much older. He told how once he was left behind in an Indian attack without his hat, and once when he was in Central America he learned that yellow fever was raging, but a kind friend lent him a hat. He also left four hundred acres of rich land, but never lived to enjoy them.

It was about 1870 that Colonel Savoy moved to Fannin County. He took on the location of the new town and saw that Mr. William B. Smith was about to lose. A deed filed in Bonham, in October 1872, shows that Savoy sold to the Transcontinental Railroad (now the Texas and Pacific) forty acres of land — this is the site on which the town stands — for the occasion to have the town named for him.
